tag: P2.18 is placed after the next PHASE heading and parses as P3 work
old: P2.18 [Owner ruling 2026-10-03, chartered out of P2.4 whose bar covered 2 of its 17 open rows] AN ABSENCE THAT READS AS A FACT, AND THE INSTRUMENTS THAT WOULD CATCH ONE.
why: L1, and both halves of this were REAL on the first attempt. A phase comes from the running PHASE heading and never from the slot number, so an item placed one line too late is P3 work wearing a P2 number — and nothing in the file looks wrong. Removing the heading line entirely is the sharpest form: the item's body survives and the parser sees no item at all.

tag: a row the clusters do not name stays on P2.4, so the item refills
why: L2 — the whole point of the ruling. P2.4's bar covers 2 of 17 open rows and every arrival that stays makes that worse; the leg asserts each remaining row is either named in a cluster or one of the three HIGH the Owner held there, so a single arrival drifting back is caught.

tag: a HIGH row the ruling held inside P2.4 leaves it
why: L2, the other direction, and it matters more than it looks: FU-346 is one of the two rows that make products/capital_fund IMPOSSIBLE TO IMPORT. The Owner ruled those stay inside P2.4 because cluster (a) is about owning or retiring what is dead, and a module nothing can import is exactly that. Rerouting it would hide a HIGH defect under a newly chartered item.

tag: a moved row carries no reason for having moved
old: "slot_source": "chartered out of P2.4 by the Owner ruling of 2026-10-03: it arrived after P2.4's bar was written and no cluster names it; its subject is an absence that reads as a fact"
why: L3. A reslot with no stated reason is how a row ends up somewhere nobody can justify later — and the currency guard exempts a row that carries a slot_source, so an empty one both loses the reason AND changes how the register treats it.

tag: P2.18's bar can be satisfied by closing rows
old:
(3) no clause
      closes on a count of rows — the clause closes when its property holds, and a row left open under a
      closed clause is named with the reason it was left.
new: (3) every row under a clause is closed.
why: L4, and it is the exact defect P2.18 was chartered to avoid. P2.4's bar was derived from the rows open when it was written and drifted until it covered 2 of 17; a new item whose clauses close on a row count would repeat that in one round. An item closes on its ACCEPT clause, and zero rows means unexamined.

tag: the new bar lists row ids, so a row cannot be moved without rewriting the bar
old: most expensive moment in a round. THREE ROWS prompted this: the absent frontend test runner,
new: most expensive moment in a round. (FU-352, FU-359, FU-365.) The absent frontend test runner,
why: L4. The register's guard only refuses an id belonging to ANOTHER item, so a bar listing its OWN rows passes it — and this round paid the cost: FU-369 could not be moved out of P2.4 until a sentence naming it was rewritten. A bar of deliverables should not care which rows sit under it today.

tag: the bar does not say where P2.4's routes go, so the sink refills after it closes
old:
ALL SEVEN OF P2.4's ROUTES COME HERE WHEN
      IT CLOSES, through `done --hand-to P2.18`
new: The routes stay where they are
why: L4. Five of P2.4's seven routes were themselves handed in when other items closed, which is how it became a sink; leaving them behind would hand the sink to whichever item inherits them next and reproduce the whole problem one slot along.

tag: the ruling block stops naming the item the split creates
old: the sixteen arrivals become P2.18 with their own ACCEPT
why: L5. A ruling that does not name what it created cannot be checked against what exists — and these rulings are constitution, which a later round may not widen, soften or reinterpret. It can only hold to them if it can tell what they produced.
